## Learning objectives

After completing this chapter, readers should be able to

- distinguish supply chain management from logistics and related functions,
- explain the value-creating role of procurement, production, distribution, and sales,
- analyze material, information, and financial flows across a supply chain,
- classify focal and polycentric supply chain structures,
- assess the implications of objectives, trade-offs, and cost structures in SCM.

## Introduction

Supply chain management is often perceived as a modern management concept. Historically, however, supply, transport, coordination, and provisioning problems have existed for millennia. The introductory lecture uses the construction of the Cheops pyramid, Hannibal’s campaign across the Alps, and Alexander the Great’s campaigns to show that large-scale supply systems long predate digital technologies and globalized sourcing. These examples are useful because they emphasize the enduring managerial problem: ensuring that the right resources are available in the right quantity, place, and time under conditions of uncertainty and interdependence [@werner2020; @kummer2022].

A modern supply chain differs from these historical examples above all in complexity, speed, and organizational fragmentation. Today’s supply chains span multiple independent firms, countries, legal systems, and digital infrastructures. As a consequence, SCM is not limited to moving goods efficiently. It is concerned with the strategic and operational design of a coordinated value-creation network that aligns procurement, production, distribution, and demand fulfillment across organizational boundaries [@chopra2022; @christopher2016].

## What is a supply chain?

A supply chain comprises all organizations, resources, activities, and information involved in transforming raw materials into products or services and delivering them to the final customer. This includes upstream suppliers, focal firms, downstream channel partners, and the interfaces through which orders, forecasts, materials, services, and payments are exchanged [@chopra2022; @stadtler2015].

The lecture juxtaposes several influential definitions. Stadtler emphasizes the integration of organizational units and the coordination of material, information, and financial flows. Hugos defines SCM as the coordination of production, inventory, location, transportation, and information in order to balance responsiveness and efficiency. Corsten and Gössinger stress sourcing, procurement, conversion, logistics, and collaboration across channel partners. Taken together, these definitions show that SCM is simultaneously process-oriented, cross-functional, and interorganizational [@stadtler2015; @hugos2018; @corsten2001].

## SCM and logistics

Although the terms are often used interchangeably in practice, logistics and supply chain management are not identical. Logistics focuses on the efficient planning, implementation, and control of the movement and storage of goods and related information. Supply chain management is broader because it also includes sourcing decisions, supplier relationships, network design, coordination mechanisms, and the alignment of supply with demand across firms [@christopher2016; @schulte2017].

This distinction matters analytically. A company may operate an efficient logistics system while still suffering from poor supply chain performance because forecasts are distorted, suppliers are badly integrated, or incentives across partners are misaligned. SCM therefore extends beyond physical flow management toward a systemic perspective on value creation and coordination [@chopra2022; @werner2020].

## Utility and value creation

The first lecture introduces the idea that supply exists in order to create utility for the customer. Building on logistics and value-chain thinking, products generate utility not only through their intrinsic properties but also through availability at the right time, in the right place, in the right quantity, and with the right information [@porter1985; @kummer2022].

This perspective is useful because it links SCM directly to customer satisfaction. A product may be technically excellent, but if it is unavailable when demanded or inaccessible through the preferred distribution channel, customer utility remains low. SCM thus contributes to property utility, time utility, place utility, information utility, and design utility by coordinating the underlying transformation and delivery processes [@christopher2016; @werner2020].

## Value creation as process

The lecture further develops this logic by modeling value creation as a sequence of transformations. Qualitative transformation changes the characteristics of an object, spatial transformation changes its location, temporal transformation ensures availability at the right time, and quantitative transformation adjusts lot size or assortment to market needs [@kummer2022; @guenther2007].

In business reality, these transformations are tightly coupled. Procurement secures inputs from upstream suppliers, production transforms them into intermediate and final outputs, distribution ensures spatial and temporal availability, and sales connects the offering to market demand. This process-oriented view is particularly helpful for teaching because it avoids reducing SCM to a purely logistical support function and instead places it at the center of coordinated value creation [@porter1985; @werner2020].

## Enterprise as an open system

A key conceptual contribution of the introductory lecture is the open systems view of the firm. Following Kummer, Grün, and Jammernegg, companies can be analyzed on a goods level, a financial level, and a planning-and-decision level. This framework emphasizes that supply chains are not just physical systems; they are also systems of information processing, decision-making, and capital commitment [@kummer2022].

This distinction is essential for SCM because many performance problems are not caused by the physical flow itself. They emerge when planning information is poor, payment structures distort incentives, or decision rights are badly assigned across organizations. The open-systems perspective therefore supports a more complete diagnosis of supply chain performance and failure [@stadtler2015; @werner2020].

## Flows in supply chains

A foundational SCM perspective is to analyze supply chains through three interconnected flows: material flow, information flow, and financial flow. The lecture explicitly emphasizes that these flows are initiated at different points, move in different directions, and must be coordinated rather than assumed to be naturally synchronized [@kummer2022; @chopra2022].

### Material flow

Material flow describes the physical movement of raw materials, components, intermediate goods, and finished products from upstream suppliers through production and distribution to the final customer. In many supply chains, reverse flows such as returns, repairs, remanufacturing, or recycling must also be considered [@christopher2016; @werner2020].

### Information flow

Information flow includes customer orders, forecasts, stock information, capacity data, shipment notifications, and point-of-sale signals. It plays a critical role because physical flow can only be coordinated effectively when planning and execution rely on timely and accurate information. The literature repeatedly shows that poor information sharing amplifies variability, contributes to the bullwhip effect, and increases inventories and stockouts [@lee1997; @chopra2022].

### Financial flow

Financial flow includes invoices, payments, payment terms, trade credit, and other funding mechanisms along the supply chain. From a managerial perspective, this is highly relevant because working capital, liquidity, and cost allocation strongly influence sourcing and inventory decisions. Material can move downstream while money moves upstream, often with long delays between delivery and payment [@werner2020; @christopher2016].

## Supply chain structures

The lecture distinguishes focal from polycentric supply chains. In focal supply chains, one dominant company controls crucial interfaces, sets standards, and often coordinates the network. Typical examples include automotive value chains or platform-centered ecosystems in consumer electronics, where a focal firm strongly influences design, scheduling, and supplier behavior [@chopra2022; @werner2020].

Polycentric supply chains, by contrast, are characterized by distributed competencies, greater specialization, and a more balanced distribution of power. Coordination is less strongly centered in one actor and more dependent on negotiated interfaces, relational governance, and collaborative planning [@christopher2016; @stadtler2015].

This distinction matters because governance mechanisms differ significantly. Focal supply chains tend to rely more heavily on standardization, contractual discipline, and performance monitoring. Polycentric systems require stronger capabilities in collaboration, conflict resolution, and network governance.

## Examples and network thinking

The lecture asks students to map supply chains for products such as Coca-Cola, Patagonia apparel, Canyon bicycles, and Ritter Sport chocolate. This exercise is didactically powerful because it forces students to identify raw materials, intermediate steps, geographic allocation, and the logistics links that connect production stages [@werner2020; @schulte2017].

Such examples also demonstrate why the term supply chain can be misleading if interpreted too literally. Most real systems are not simple linear chains but networks with multiple tiers, many-to-many supplier relations, alternative transport paths, and feedback loops. The ability to think in networks rather than in sequential chains is one of the core analytical skills in SCM [@stadtler2015; @chopra2022].

## The supply chain surplus perspective

The lecture highlights a central insight from Chopra and Meindl: total supply chain profit equals customer revenue minus the total cost incurred across all participating processes and partners. This implies that maximizing the profit of individual actors does not automatically maximize the performance of the supply chain as a whole [@chopra2022].

This perspective is fundamental because it explains why decentralized decision-making often creates inefficiencies. Local optimization may increase one actor’s accounting result while reducing network-level performance through excess stock, poor service, or duplicated activities. The concept of supply chain surplus therefore provides a normative benchmark for system-wide optimization [@chopra2022; @cachon2005].

## Objectives and target dimensions

The lecture introduces a classical target system for logistics and SCM consisting of lead time, delivery reliability, delivery quality, flexibility or resilience, information quality, and cost. These dimensions remain highly relevant because they capture both efficiency and service aspects of supply chain performance [@schulte2017; @werner2020].

Importantly, these dimensions are interdependent. Reducing lead times may require higher inventory or faster transport modes. Increasing flexibility may lower capacity utilization. Improving service reliability may increase redundancy and therefore cost. SCM is therefore characterized by persistent target conflicts rather than by a single dominant objective [@christopher2016; @chopra2022].

## Trade-offs and logistics cost

The introductory lecture explicitly addresses conflicting cost components in logistics and SCM. This is an essential theme because logistics costs are never determined in isolation. Warehousing, transportation, lot sizing, safety stock, and service design interact in ways that make local cost minimization potentially harmful at the system level [@schulte2017; @werner2020].

The literature emphasizes that transparency of logistics cost functions is often limited by data availability, time lags, allocation problems, and stochastic influences. As a result, managerial decisions are often made under uncertainty and with incomplete cost visibility. This is one reason why SCM relies not only on accounting information but also on analytical modeling and scenario-based reasoning [@guenther2007; @werner2020].

## Supply chain costing

The Apple iPod example used in the lecture illustrates how supply chain costing can reveal the distribution of value creation across countries, stages, and actors. The example makes clear that manufacturing and assembly costs represent only part of the total value logic. Design, branding, retailing, and channel coordination can account for a substantial share of the captured margin [@dedrick2010].

From a teaching perspective, such examples are important because they show students that global supply chains cannot be understood through production cost alone. Costing must account for procurement, production, distribution, retailing, and margin capture across the full chain. This broad view prepares the ground for later discussions of strategic fit, responsiveness, and network design.

## Positioning of Chapter 1

The first chapter establishes the conceptual vocabulary required for the remainder of the book. It defines the object of analysis, explains how value is created in supply chains, introduces the relevant flows and structures, and clarifies why objectives and costs must be considered at the system level rather than within isolated functions [@chopra2022; @werner2020].

This foundation is necessary before strategic choices can be discussed. Once the supply chain is understood as a coordinated but tension-laden network, the next question is how it should be designed to match customer requirements, uncertainty, and competitive positioning.
